title: “Power” Fireside Chat: Professor Jeff Pfeffer and Dean Jon Levin
transcript: [MUSIC] So thank you all for being here. And now, I'm going to bring up Jeff Pfeffer. So while Jeff's walking up, actually, let me just ask, how many people took Jeff Pfeffer's Paths to Power class? Nice, okay, that's a lot. Jeff, you got a lot of fans here, I hope. >> [APPLAUSE] >> Have a seat. So let me introduce Jeff for those of you who, everyone knows Jeff, but let me introduce him for the people who might not know him. So Jeff is the Thomas D professor at the GSB. He's been on the GSB, should I say it or is that okay? >> Yeah, he's been with GSB faculty since 1979. Here's taught, I was trying to calculate it this morning, I think he's taught about 4,000 students in the MBA and MSx programs in the Paths to Power class. That was my calculation. And here's also got an online version that he teaches in our Stanford LEAD program. And I think he's probably doubled it online, is my guess. So he's taught a lot of people, he's had tremendous influence in his thinking about organizational behavior. And on Tuesday night, Jeff received the highest with the internal award. We give to faculty the Davis Award and we give Jeff the Davis Award. And one of his colleagues describe Jeff as being both an icon and an iconoclast, okay? Icon in the sense of he's a giant as a teacher and a thinker in organizational behavior. And iconoclast, well, you're going to see when we have this discussion, he thinks differently. And Jeff, thank you for doing this. >> Thank you, it's a pleasure to be with you. >> [APPLAUSE] >> And consistent with my Path to Power principles, you're my favorite thing. >> [LAUGH] >> Okay, we have some prepared questions, but I'm just going to dispense with them, and I- >> [LAUGH] >> Because I know it'll be more interesting just to chat. So actually, let's start with power. >> Sure. >> So one of the things that you often say is that people are uncomfortable with the concept of power, that's been one of your themes. Explain that. >> So actually in 1979, Rosabeth Moss Kanter, who taught and still teaches at Harvard Business School, wrote an article entitled Power of Failure in Management Circuits. And talked about the fact that in those days, and I think it's still true, you can talk about money, and you can talk about sex, and on certain TV channels, that's all they talk about. But the people aren't comfortable talking about power. She called power the organization's last dirty secrets, and I believe that that is still true. People would like to believe that the world is a just and fair place, that people get what they deserve, that everything works out at the end. What's the line from the Best Exotic Marigold Hotel? That everything works out in the end. If it's not worked out, it's not yet the end, there is something to that effect. So I think power does make people uncomfortable. I don't think power is the last dirty secret, I think it's the secret to success. If the business, as you know I say all the time, Stanford Business School's motto is change lives, change organizations, change the world. If change were going to happen without the exertion of power and influence, it would have happened already. If we are going to, in fact, change life, change organizations, and change the world, you're going to need power because things are the way they are for a reason. They're in some state of equilibrium. If you want to get them out of this, you want to get them into disequilibrium, you need influence. >> All right, you've written a couple of books about power, and the most recent one is the Seven Laws of Power. >> Seven rules. >> Seven Rules of Power, tell us what they are. >> Sure, so I've written actually, I think now four or five, depending upon your count, books about power. It goes back to 1981 when my first book was called Power, and I wrote Managing With Power and a bunch of others, and including my favorite, which was Leadership BS, which is why you need a book about power. But in any event, the seven rules of power are, and I think the first rule is the first rule for reason. The first rule of power is get out of your own way, that many people are inhibited. I think particularly for women, if you tell them they're ambitious, they would take that as an insult. It's often intended as an insult. I think we are reluctant, both men and women, to lean into our ambition. We are reluctant to do what it takes to be powerful. We are oftentimes overly concerned with being liked. My friend Gary Loveman, who ran Caesars for many years has this wonderful saying, which I have on video, if you want to be liked like a dog, a dog will love you unconditionally. Your job as a leader is not necessarily to win a popularity contest, but to do what needs to be done to make the organization successful and achieve your agenda. So I think the first rule is get out of your own way. Another way in which people get in their own way is that they live with some form of imposter syndrome. They believe they don't deserve the power that they have, or they describe themselves in self-deprecating ways. And my favorite story, a woman comes to see me, she's working at this company that has all the I's, and she has run a market research program, which has made the company a lot of money. But one of her peers has gone to their common boss and said, I want you to have to report to me, which is a smart move because that way I'll be able to take a credit for her work. And she said to the room, she says, what should I do? And I said, well, before want to do anything, I want to tell you in the ten minutes you've been here, I've heard many times that you're the only woman, that you're the youngest person in this group of peers and the boss. And you're the least senior in the company. I said, let me give you three other descriptors. You're the most analytically skilled. You're the only one who graduated from a prestigious business school. And you've run the project that's made the most money. And she sits up a little straighter, Taiwanese American woman. And I said six adjectives, you get to pick which three. You want to describe yourself in ways, I'm youngest, I'm least senior, ways that make you less deserving, smartest, prestigious business school, most deserving. Get out of your own way. That's rule one. Rule two, break the rules, break the rules. If I put this in the context of social change, it would be immediate. The Late Representative John Lewis said, get into trouble, get into good trouble. Nelson Mandela, the father of South Africa, was the father of South Africa while he was in jail. Martin Luther King's letter from a Birmingham Jail was written while he was in a Birmingham Jail. You're going to change things, the status quo isn't going to like that. You need to be willing to break the rules. In strategy, if I said to you today I'm going to go into business, I'm going to make a computer the runs of Microsoft Office and Microsoft systems and it's going to be black, what's my chances of success? Close to zero, because, of course, I'm doing what everybody else does. And strategy, we understand, That you redefine industries by breaking the rules of those industries. Southwest Airlines with their turnaround times, Whole Foods was selling food that people want to eat. So it's all around breaking rules. Rule three, you want to act and speak with power. Confidence is often confused with competence. But you want to act like you know what you're doing, you want to act and speak in a powerful fashion. And that's why my colleague and your friend Deborah Gruenfeld teaches a class called acting with power, it's all about great leaders are great actors. Andy Grove, the late Andy Grove of Intel, was quoted in giving a talk in the Silicon Valley of saying oftentimes at Intel I didn't know what I was doing, but you have to act like you do. Because if you show up, any startup founder would understand. If you show up and say I have no idea what we're doing, I know we've faced some setbacks, which by the way every organization does, I'm clueless. The customers are going to leave, the employees are going to leave, the investors are going to leave. So rule two is show up, and rule three is show up with power. >> Before you go to rule four. But I want to stop you before you go to rule four because already I think everyone can see why some of what you say is controversial. So we're here in Silicon Valley and, I'll just play devil's advocate for a minute. Some people would say looking at Silicon Valley we've had too many people who are adhering to the fake it till you make it and breaking the rules in building companies, how do you respond to that? >> It's interesting, on Thursday I think of this coming week, we're going to have a series, we're going to have three of my colleagues are going to talk about bank failures. Which is interesting, because bank failures are an example of a principle which I think is highly underrated, which is the self-fulfilling prophecy. I don't understand the failure of First Republic Bank, which for many years was by far one of the highest performing banks in the United States. ROA, ROS, RO anything, highest level of customer satisfaction, wonderful bank. Except through what Robert Merton, the sociologist who invented the self-fulfilling prophecy uses this example, which is bank runs. And I see imitative behavior all the time, I wrote a post about layoffs being imitative behavior. So there is a self-fulfilling prophecy, to the extent that I believe you are successful, we, everybody in this room, is a beneficiary of the self-fulfilling prophecy. Because we have convinced people, and I believe it's true, but we have convinced people that Stanford is the best business school. We get the best students and the best faculty. If you get the best students and the best faculty, you become the best business school. And what was once a whatever, a dream or a myth, becomes in fact reality. If you believe that First Republic is going to fail and you pull $100 billion of deposits in one quarter out of First Republic Bank, nobody can stand up to that and so First Republic fails. I by the way, to this day, am a customer of First Republic. And I dread Chase, because Chase has perfected the art of all large banks which is providing no customer service, but it turns out if you're a monopoly it doesn't matter. >> [LAUGH] >> So I'm a huge believer in the self-fulfilling prophecy. And so yes, it is the job of a, what is it, 70, 80, 90% of new ventures fail. If I say to you, John, I want you to come into my company. You're a smart guy, you have a PhD, you've been dean at Stanford, but if you decide to make a career change you want to work for me. [LAUGH] >> I'm ready, give me the pitch. >> By the way, 90% of new companies fail. I am a new company, therefore you have a 90% chance of failing, would you like to join me? I don't think you're going to join. Part of life is convincing people that the impossible is in fact possible. My dear friend who we gave the Arbuckle Award to some years ago, the famous Laura Esterman, Who's changing medicine, who's changing breast cancer, who's changing things in a profound way. She has been quoted, because she's on a video because I recorded her that particular day she came to my class, is convincing people that what they didn't think could happen can happen. That's how change occurs, it is easy. My friend Rudy Crew also comes to my class, New York Schools Chancellor, wonderful man. My job, he said, is to convince. Urban education in this country is a colossal, catastrophic failure, probably worse than in the city of San Francisco where they recalled most of the school board. My job is to convince people who have given up, given up on children of color, on immigrant children, that in fact these children can have the same education that we give to the children of privilege, and that they can achieve to the same level. Now, by the way, we haven't yet succeeded in doing that. And so to some extent Rudy Crew and Laura Esterman are telling people things that do not exist, but if you don't believe that they can exist you will never try. >> Mm-hm. >> We're only through rule three, but let's. [LAUGH] >> You want to go through the rest of the rules quickly, because I've got so many more questions. >> Sure, okay, this is wonderful, we're going to talk. >> We'll talk for hours, we'll be here till 9:00, it's great. >> [LAUGH] >> Rule four. So rule three is act and speak with power. Rule four is to build a strong personal brand. Just as Coca-Cola, and First Republic, and Chase, and everybody else, Southwest Airlines, has built a brand, you need to build a brand. You need to stand for something, you need to have a succinct way of describing what you do that integrates your life with what you're currently doing. As my friends from the private boys school that I went to many years ago will tell you, I was a troublemaker then, I still am, it's fine, that's my brand. [LAUGH] Rule five is network relentlessly. If management, slash, leadership is getting things done it's through other people, you need to know a lot of other people. So the more people you know, the more stuff you can get done, you want to network relentlessly. Rule six is use your power. When somebody makes you dean, or somebody makes you CEO, or somebody makes you president, or somebody makes you school superintendent, they have expectations that you're going to do something, use that power. Jim Collins talks about getting the right people on the bus. If you look at what Amir Rubin did first at Stanford Health Care, and now at One Medical which was bought by Amazon and Amir made $114 million, which makes him my closest, richest friend. I have closer friends, I have richer friends, if you put the two together. >> [LAUGH] >> [LAUGH] If you put the two together then multiply the two, it's Amir. >> [CROSSTALK] >> And basically you look at Stanford Health Care, 70% of the people three levels down were different after about three years, you want the right people. Jim Collins, get the right people on the bus, you want to use your power You want to get things done. Nobody has put you in this job to do nothing, you need to use your power to make things happen. And Rule 7, which is probably the most controversial rule of all, people say to me, you've told me things to do. By the way, none of these things strike me as very controversial. I mean, getting out of your own way seems common sense. All this stuff seems pretty common sense. But in any event, it's got a social science ground as well. Rule 7 is that once you have power and wealth, people will forgive or forget how you got it. And that is, I think, also demonstrated every day. I began this chapter with the example of Lindsey Graham. Lindsey Graham was the ultimate never Trumper, and now he's got his lips firmly affixed to, well, we won't go there. [LAUGH] Donald Trump, many people did not like Donald Trump. Business people did not like Donald Trump. But the day Donald Trump became elected, and after it was clear that he wasn't going to quit or do something or whatever, that he was actually going to be not only a president, but a president who uses power, a lot of the business leaders changed their opinion of him. So Rule 7 is you need to be successful, and once you're successful you'll have more friends than you want. >> [LAUGH] >> So, Jeff, I sometimes think of you as the, and this is actually a compliment. >> [LAUGH] No compliment begins with a statement that this is going to be a compliment. >> [LAUGH] >> I sometimes think of Jeff as the Henry Kissinger of organizational behavior, the real politic sort of view of organizational behavior. By the way, Jeff, if you are still teaching when you're 98 or 99 like Henry Kissinger, that'll be great. So we need to aim for that. Let me ask you about the class. So your syllabus starts by saying, this class is not for everyone. >> That's correct. >> Tell us what you mean by that. >> Well, so one year I was teaching, and there were some students that it turns out that about three of them were sitting together. And every class, because they were sitting kind of right in the middle and about the third row back, and every class they looked like they were having some very painful medical procedure done to them. >> [LAUGH] >> Pick your favorite one. And at the end of the class, it's also clear that they did not learn anything. So in order to get the benefit out of pass the power, which as you know has an enormous waiting list, in order to get the benefit out of pass the power you have to be open. And by the way, I think this is true for any class, I think this is true for economics. I mean, if I came into a class, in the microeconomics, or for that matter, macroeconomics, and said, I find the principles that you're teaching abhorrent. And therefore, I won't engage intellectually with the material- >> Who could possibly think that? >> I don't know, [LAUGH], you wouldn't learn anything. So you have to be open to the experience, you have to be open to learning. And if you are, many people have gotten enormous benefit out of the class. And if you're not, it's going to be a horrible experience. And it's an elective, you don't have to take it. Take something that's more to your liking, whatever. So that's why I put that in. So to get people to understand, I mean, this class has been taught for a long time, I'm not likely to change. If you don't like me, you don't like the material, don't take it. It's not a problem. I'm not going to be personally offended. >> You've taught the class for a long time. And this group captures about half of that period, how have the students changed? >> Always for the better. >> [LAUGH] >> I could tell you how the class has changed. So some years ago, I had lunch with Carol Robin, and I said to her, how do I make this class better? And she said, you at the moment have a class in applied social science, you need a class that deals with what the students are actually most interested in, which is, of course, themselves. And so with the- >> Did you all catch that? >> [LAUGH] It's true, we're all interested in ourselves. And so I basically redid the entire class. I redid the cases, so that the cases, we no longer have Robert Moses, or Lyndon Johnson, or readings on Robert McNamara, all these other interesting people. We have readings on, again, we have cases on people who are like them, five to ten years out. Some of them from Harvard Business School, some from Stanford Business School. But people who they can, entrepreneurs, my friend, Jason Calacanis, the king of angel investing, people that they can kind of see and relate to. That's the first big change. And the second big change is I, with the school's generous support, which I thank Paul Oyer for every minute, and thank you for today, we have, coaching, executive coaching. Six executive coaches work with this class, who provide an extraordinary level of feedback on the eight self-reflective exercises that I give the students to do, which includes build a personal brand. Who do you need to network with? How are you going to meet them? What are the personal attributes that you need to change? How are you going to change them during the ten weeks? And it is amazing to me what you can accomplish in eight to ten weeks with an enormous level of feedback, and whatever. So the class has changed. And because I think the class has changed, I think the student experience has changed for the better, I hope. And so that's how I think things have changed. I think the other change in the student body, which I'm sure you've seen, is we live in a world of much more social consciousness than I think there was 20 or 30 years ago. Frankly because we live in a world that's a hell of a lot more dangerous than it was 20 or 30 years ago. 20 or 30 years ago, you did not have a land war in Europe. 20 or 30 years ago, you did not have, or if you had it, it was not as visible, mass shootings all the time, police doing what they do to people of color, etc. So 20 or 30 years ago you didn't have the prospect of Donald Trump being president again. So we live in a much more dangerous world, and in a much more interesting and challenging world, including the change that you've described. Including artificial intelligence, where now, apparently, the father of artificial intelligence is worried that it's going to do all this harm and damage, whatever. So we live in a dangerous and interesting challenging world with the climate crisis, in school of environmental studies, all this stuff. And so I think the students reflect the world that we live in, in the sense that I think they have a much higher level of social awareness and social conscience. They also, I think, are more stressed, and I think that's true for the undergraduates at Stanford as well. >> So that actually picks up another topic which you've worked on, which I would love to get you to share with the group, which is the issues of health in the workplace, and particularly mental health. So that's been a big topic for you recently. >> Yes. >> Maybe share a little bit of the thinking you've done. because it's been, in a way, kind of an unusual topic for a business school professor to think about. >> I guess it's unusual. And everything I do, I think makes all perfect sense. So it's not [LAUGH] unusual for me. I wrote a book in 2018 called Dying for a Paycheck. Which actually had influence on the Surgeon General of the United States, it had influence on people actually all over the world. And it is the workplace, according to my colleague, Stefano Xenios and Joel Go, doctoral student in the school who helped me with the research, the workplace is the fifth leading cause of death in the United States, responsible for 120,000 excess deaths a year. And by the way, my friends in human resources when that book came out said your numbers are way off that they're much too low. The general consensus is that, and this is also, by the way, pre-COVID, where the stress has gone up. Stress is not healthy. If you go read the medical literature, you can find that stress is not healthy in two ways. Number one, it leads to unhealthy behaviors, which has been studied for decades, smoking, drinking, drug abuse, and overeating, etc. Anyway, stress is also unhealthy because they have now actually mapped in a variety of ways the effect of stress and depression on the central nervous system which regulates almost every chemical in your body, including hormones and then oxycontin, and cortisol, and all of these things. And so we know that stress is harmful, we know that depression is harmful, we know the workplace because of studies that Gallup has done everybody else has done, is a source of stress and depression. And so therefore, if you want to fix the escalating healthcare COC crisis around the world, you actually have to address the workplace. I also my favorite chapter in Dying for Workplaces chapter seven, which is why people stay in workplaces that they know are killing them. And one simple answer as a friend of mine said to me, Jeffery, finding another job is a job in and of itself. I am so exhausted mentally and physically that I can't get out. It's kind of depressing, anyway, I don't want to depress anybody today. >> [LAUGH] >> It's a happy weekend for, that's a- >> [LAUGH] >> But I would point out that the one thing, I mean, in that book I quoted the New York Times article, where I don't know if you know this, at that time at least the Palo Alto Medical Foundation had a van that went around to high tech workplaces. Because the engineers making dating apps, I guess thought that they were doing work too important to go and see the doctor. And in any event, the guy who ran the Palo Alto Van, Pam Foundation Van at that time, said, I've seen 30 year old engineers with 50 year old bodies. He said if you're a 30 year old engineer with a 50 year old body, you're not going to get that 30 year old body back. It is physically, physiologically impossible. So, basically, I've I recently written a LinkedIn post about this also, prevention is a hell of a lot more cost effective and a whole lot more effective than remediation. And this is true in health and it's true in mental health. That intervening early, I am doing a paper now believe it or not with the CEO of Mural health, they provide mental health benefits. And he shows that their programs prevent people from going from a state of mild crisis to deep crisis. And that's I think great because for both physical health, I mean, if you're pre-diabetic, it's better to not become diabetic. If you're pre-depression, it's better to not become depressed. Because once you are in a state of acute physical or behavioral ill health, it's very hard and much more expensive to reverse it. So this is kind of one of the current things I'm working on, I work on a few other things. >> If you all want to read something really excellent that Jeff wrote recently, he has an article in McKinsey Quarterly from a couple of years ago about, I think it's the first article out about workplace mental health and it's really a good read actually. It starts with the story of one of our alums and lecturers, a fellow named Lenny Mendonca. And it's really impactful. And the Vivek Murthy, who is the Surgeon General of the United States, by the way he's an MBA even though he's a Surgeon General, just not a Stanford MBA, unfortunately. He really picked up on that, what Jeff has done and now has been doing a lot of mental health stuff. Jeff, let me ask a question about, it'll be relevant for this audience. So in your class, the students spent a lot of time thinking about individually what will be their path to power. >> Correct. >> And I always tell you how much I enjoy when someone comes to visit me and says, let me tell you how things have worked out either in accordance or not in accordance with my plan and Jeff's class. Often it's in accordance, actually, which is great. So now you've got a group in front of you, they're one year out, or five years out, or ten years out, or 20 years out, what would you tell them about their path to power starting here? >> That's a great question. So I often will get comments sometimes from people I'm connected to on Linkedin or other people. And they say to me, I wish I had known this ten or 20 years ago, or 30 years ago. It's like too late for me or whatever, and I tell them it's never too late. It is never too late. It is never too late to master the rules of power. It is never too late to start doing it. And so that would be my word of advice. You don't have to do it, it's nice if you started, in the womb or whenever some of these people that, when Ben Johnson that was I think a natural politician that it started early, but you don't have to start early, it is never too late. You all have, particularly, since everybody in this room is younger than me, then you all have a lot of your life left in front of you and you can always learn things. By the way, not just power things, but other things as well, that you can use. I suspect you would tell people that it's never too late to learn principles of economics, and my colleagues in finance will tell you it's never too late to learn the principles of finance and operations, management, etc., etc. Because you have time left in front of you in which you can take this learning and apply it to all the various aspects of your life, so that would be my, go learn it today. I think the bookstore is supposed to be selling copies, that bookstore typically has three copies of my book. So, they made them now stock more but I doubt it. Because, of course, Stanford Bookstore is no longer a bookstore if you haven't visited it recently. >> It's a great read, it's not too long, the new one, so you can get through it in a couple of evenings. Let's open it up for some questions and see what's on people's minds. So, feel free to ask Jeff anything. >> So Jeff, a lot of your work in a lot of the class is on individual power. And something that's been really interesting in the last year to two is the rise of unions and bringing back this idea of collective power. So, I'm curious because we also don't really do it in the business school curriculum either and so now you have this crop of business leaders that have zero idea on how to deal with collective power. So curious, one, for your take on what is kind of spurring the rise of collective power and two, advice on how leaders should think about this. >> Thank you, that's some interesting questions. So. There is a lot more publicity about the rise of unions than there is actually the rise of unions. I was notorious for when I taught the class here on human resources, which I used to do, which at one point was a core class actually, having a session on unions, which made me, I think, relatively unique. Unions are largely disappeared from all business school curricula, mostly because students would ask me why did they need to know about unions? And I would tell them that they weren't always going to work just in the United States and that there were other countries. Such as Germany, which has co-determination, Singapore, which actually has a reasonably strong union movement, whatever. So yes, there's a lot of publicity about the unions that have organized at Amazon and Starbucks that they've tried to organize. But the percentage of people in unions has continued unfortunately to decline. And in a moment of course, things that give my poor dean heartburn, Stanford, as you know, is facing a union organizing campaign. And I would urge you to follow Stanford's response and watch what they do. >> [LAUGH] >> And watch what they do. When the clerical workers tried to organize a union many decades ago, Stanford hired Littler, Mendelson, and which is known as a union-busting firm. The graduate students are now thinking about unionizing at Stanford. And the graduate students have asked the administration to recognize the union without an election, you can picture what the response would be. And we will see what Stanford does, my forecast is It will not be nice. >> [LAUGH] >> Because one of the things that we have whether there is a. Kruger and Dunning wrote this wonderful, fabulous article called Unskilled and Unaware of It. Most people believe that they are, and certainly most leaders believe that they are smart. And they've gotten to where they are because they're smart and that therefore they know better than everybody else. And I can guarantee you, and this is not a shocking statement, that the people who run Stanford University believe that they know better for what's good for the graduate students than the graduate students do. And that would be true for all of you, that if I asked you to prescribe for me, or for John, or for anybody in this room, what they should do, you would immediately respond to that because you're smart, talented people. And so we're going to be smart, talented people, we're going to tell the graduate students what we think they need, which is, by the way, not a union. So watch carefully, watch the Stanford Daily, it's interesting. I get a daily Stanford Daily feed, it's great. >> [LAUGH] >> So that's a long way of saying that collective power I think is important, but it is hard to organize. By the way, the decline in unions has occurred worldwide, not just in the United States, because we've diffused our ideas around the world and so now we've got this interesting issue. But the wonderful thing about my job and being who I am, is that the most interesting human beings in the world reach out to me. I am personal friends with the former head of the Service Employees International Union. The woman who organized with her partner the recall of the San Francisco School Board reached out to me over last Christmas. When there was the shooting in the Marjory Parkland schools, one of the student leaders reached out and said you know about power, tell me what to do. I said on the day a politician loses their election because they did not support reasonable gun regulations things will change, and until then nothing will change, not the moving speeches or anything else. And so we need collective power, we need the hard work. >> Let me, just to add a couple of things to build on what you said, Jeff. One is, if you read the media, you hear a lot about how everybody on a campus thinks the same way, that there's this sort of homogeneity that has crept into university thinking. Let me just tell you that among the GSB faculty that is definitely not the case. >> [LAUGH] >> Similarly with willing to speak up. And just two more things I'll just add. That I actually do encourage you to follow the unionization issue. It's quite interesting that many years ago, at many public universities the graduate students unionized as employees. And it never happened at private institutions because the National Labor Relations Board had not decided whether grad students were employees or students under the National Labor Relations Act. And about two years ago when the Biden administration came in they changed the rules and made it clear that they would recognize unions at private institutions. And pretty much all of our peer institutions, the grad students have unionized. At Stanford, it's not necessarily MBA professional students, not necessarily MBA students, it's people who do work for the university as research assistants and TAs. But there is a drive now to unionize at Stanford and they're likely to have an election this quarter actually, and that will be an uncertain change. It's too new a phenomenon to see sort of what that would bring, but that is an ongoing thing right now at Stanford so it's an interesting thing to keep an eye on. By the way, on unions, it is true that we do not have a class on unions. But we at least did have a big event on unions earlier this year as part of the Corporations and Society Initiative, and it was quite a robust discussion.
